notes: Sparrmannia was a plausible Malvaceae clue because Vogel's pollen-flower literature and later sources describe conspicuous yellow outer structures plus fertile inner stamens. Direct morphology resolves the yellow outer structures as sterile staminodes or sterile outer stamens that mimic pollen, while the inner stamens carry the transferable pollen. This does not establish the strict two-fertile-pollen-fate heteranthery state used for U3, so the species is retained as an explicit false-positive rejection.

Pseudocorchorus is now the strongest Malvaceae lineage clue. Pre-2010 morphology records zygomorphic flowers, nearly all stamens inserted unilaterally, and elongated subbasifixed poricidal anthers; later synthesis places Pseudocorchorus explicitly in the buzz-pollination/heteranthery monosymmetry context. These traits match the 2010 review's Malvaceae family profile much better than Sparrmannia. However six Pseudocorchorus species were recognized, and no source-secure species-level two-functional-stamen-type receipt has yet identified which single Malvaceae species the review counted.

Pre-2010 sources establish pollen-only reward, poricidal anthers, buzz pollination and quantitative pollen removal/deposition. However Poppendieck's 1981 genus treatment describes Cochlospermum stamens as equal, whereas Panama descriptions report longer outer stamens. No functional two-type heteranthery receipt has been recovered, so this candidate remains open but weakened.

Amoreuxia is the stronger Bixaceae heteranthery candidate: pre-2010 treatments describe two stamen sets differing in filament length and anther colour, with poricidal anthers and zygomorphic flowers. A. palmatifida specifically has distal short yellow-anther stamens and proximal long dark-red-anther stamens. Because the review does not state that Bixaceae has only one heterantherous species, this strong species-level evidence cannot by itself identify the Table S1 representative.

Manning & Brothers 1986 directly state that heteranthery is marked in D. anastrepta: the anticous anther pair is much reduced and produces little or no yellow pollen, whereas the posticous pair associated with the stigma produces copious grey-green pollen. Diascia is compatible with APG-III Scrophulariaceae. The exact Table S1 representative identity remains unresolved because the review does not establish a unique one-species Scrophulariaceae case.

Agalinis was historically treated near Scrophulariaceae and has dimorphic stamens, but modern placement is Orobanchaceae and a direct functional study reports no division of labour typical of heteranthery.
Pre-2010 literature documents specialized buzz-pollination mechanisms in Pedicularis under older Scrophulariaceae usage. APG III places Pedicularis in Orobanchaceae.
Torenia can show heteranthery-like functional differentiation, but the recovered evidence is post-2010 and APG III treats the lineage outside Scrophulariaceae.
